opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way Jensen sees it, and the way I've come to understand it over the years, is that AI has gone through a few waves. First there was perception AI, learning to recognize images, speech, and so on. Then came generative AI, where models can create text, images, and video. The next frontier is physical AI: systems that understand the physical world, reason about it, and act in it. That means robots, autonomous vehicles, smart factories, anything that has to interact with reality rather than just pixels or tokens.

So his expectation for our team, as I understand it, is to help build the foundation for that era. Not one robot or one application, but the core technology that the whole ecosystem can build on. That's why we focus on things like world foundation models, the Cosmos effort being one example. The idea is that if you want a robot or a car to behave intelligently, it needs some internal model of how the world works: physics, cause and effect, how objects move, what happens when you push something. Collecting enough real-world data to learn all of that is extremely expensive, and sometimes dangerous. So we want models that can simulate and generate realistic worlds, so developers can train and test their systems at scale.

Jensen thinks very long-term, and he likes to work on problems that are hard and where NVIDIA can make a unique contribution. Physical AI fits that. It needs enormous compute, it needs simulation, it needs graphics. All of that is in NVIDIA's DNA. So I see our role partly as researchers pushing the state of the art, and partly as builders making tools and models open and useful for others. He often says we should do things that wouldn't happen unless we did them. For physical AI, I think that's the spirit: lay down the infrastructure so that thousands of companies and researchers can go build the robots and autonomous systems of the future.

Personally, I find it exciting, because I started in computer vision and generative models, and now those threads are coming together into something that could actually change how machines work in the real world.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to say it is that Jensen doesn't give you a roadmap. He gives you a direction and a very high bar, and then he expects you to figure out the path.

When we started the Physical AI effort, the framing from him was essentially: the next wave of AI is not going to live only inside a chat window. It has to understand the physical world, understand physics, understand how things move and interact, and eventually drive robots, autonomous vehicles, factories, everything with a body. Language models got their power from an enormous amount of text on the internet. There is no equivalent internet of physical experience. So his expectation for us was, in a sense, to go build that missing ingredient.

That is where Cosmos came from, the world foundation models. The idea is that if you can build a model that generates and simulates the physical world faithfully, you can create the data that robots need to learn from, you can let a robot imagine the consequences of an action before taking it, and you can evaluate policies in simulation rather than only in the real world, which is slow and expensive and sometimes dangerous.

What I have learned about Jensen's expectations is that they are long-term and very demanding at the same time. He is extremely patient about the mission. He will say this is a ten-year thing, maybe longer. But he is completely impatient about the pace of execution. He wants to see progress every week, and he reads the details. He will ask about a benchmark or a failure case, and you had better know the answer.

The other thing he pushes is that we should not build research for its own sake. He always asks who the customer is, who will actually use this. So we open-source the models, we work with robotics companies, with the autonomous driving team, with partners who are deploying things in the real world. The research has to turn into something that other people can build on. If it is not useful to them, it is not done.

So if I summarize his expectation in one sentence: solve the problem that nobody has solved yet, do it in a way that the whole industry can stand on, and move faster than you think you can.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that he wants us to help AI move beyond the digital world and become useful in the physical world. That means more than recognizing objects or generating a convincing video. A system needs to understand how things move, how they interact, and what might happen when it takes an action.

For our team, I think the challenge is to turn that ambition into capabilities we can demonstrate and improve. Can a model learn something about the world that helps a robot make better decisions? Can we use simulation to explore situations that would be difficult to collect in reality? And can those capabilities transfer to real environments?

I would frame the expectation as both ambitious and practical: push the research forward, but keep asking whether it helps a physical system do something useful.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I understand it, he expects us to turn advances in AI into capabilities that work in the physical world. A model can produce a convincing answer on a screen, but a robot has to understand what is happening around it, choose an action, and deal with the consequences. That raises the bar for reliability.

For our team, that means connecting perception, reasoning, and action, and building a way to train and evaluate those capabilities. Simulation is an important part of that: how can a system learn from many situations before it encounters them in the real world?

Ultimately, I think the expectation is to build a foundation that other people can use to create useful physical AI systems. The measure of success is whether those systems can perform meaningful tasks reliably.
